title: He Is Fifteen. He Won Five Awards. He Broke Chris Gayle’s Record. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi Has Rewritten the IPL.
excerpt: The boy from Tajpur, Bihar, became the youngest Orange Cap winner in IPL history, swept the MVP, Emerging Player, Super Striker, and Most Sixes awards, and broke a record that stood for thirteen years — all before his sixteenth birthday.
body:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi collected five individual awards at the IPL 2026 ceremony in Ahmedabad on Sunday night. He is fifteen years old.

The Rajasthan Royals opener won the **Orange Cap** (776 runs in 16 matches), the **Most Valuable Player** award (436.5 impact points), the **Emerging Player of the Season**, the **Super Striker of the Season** (strike rate 237.30), and the **Angel One Super Sixes of the Season** (72 sixes). No player in IPL history has swept all five in a single campaign.

## The Record That Stood for Thirteen Years

Chris Gayle hit 59 sixes for Royal Challengers Bangalore in IPL 2012. That record had survived Virat Kohli’s 973-run 2016 season, AB de Villiers at his devastating peak, and every power-hitter the tournament has produced since. Sooryavanshi obliterated it with 72 maximums — thirteen more than Gayle — while batting at an average of 48.50 and a strike rate that would be absurd for a video game, let alone a fifteen-year-old facing Jasprit Bumrah and Rashid Khan in real time.

His century against Sunrisers Hyderabad came off 36 balls. His 97 in the Eliminator came off 29. He scored over 500 runs in the powerplay alone, a phase of the innings where international bowlers are supposed to have the advantage.

## From Tajpur to Ahmedabad

Sooryavanshi was born on March 27, 2011, in Tajpur, a town in the Samastipur district of Bihar — one of India’s poorest states. His father Sanjiv, himself an aspiring cricketer, began training him at four. By eight, the two were making a 100-kilometre round trip on alternate days from Samastipur to Patna so Vaibhav could train at Manish Ojha’s GenNex Cricket Academy.

He made his Ranji Trophy debut at twelve. He was the youngest player ever signed in an IPL auction at thirteen, bought by Rajasthan Royals for ₹1.1 crore. He became the youngest centurion in IPL history at fourteen during IPL 2025. And in February 2026, he smashed 175 off 80 balls — including 15 sixes — in the Under-19 World Cup final against England to lead India to the title.

When Rahul Dravid asked the teenager what his game plan was during a Rajasthan Royals camp, the reply was instant: “If I get the first ball, I’ll hit the first ball.”

## What the Numbers Actually Mean

The raw statistics do not capture what Sooryavanshi did to the rhythm of IPL 2026. He did not merely accumulate — he terrorised. Bowlers who tried yorkers found them dispatched over midwicket. Short balls disappeared over square leg. His left-handed stance and low backlift generated bat speed that biomechanics experts have compared to early Sachin Tendulkar, but with a six-hitting frequency Tendulkar never approached in T20 cricket.

Sachin himself praised the 29-ball 97 in the Eliminator. Harsha Bhogle could barely contain himself during the awards ceremony. Ravi Shastri, who has interviewed every great of the modern era, found himself interviewing a tenth-grader collecting more trophies than most careers accumulate.

## The Diaspora Watches

For NRI cricket fans who set 3 AM alarms to catch IPL matches from the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, Sooryavanshi has become something larger than a cricket story. He is a Bihar story — a reminder that Indian cricket’s talent pipeline now reaches deep into states that historically produced bureaucrats and migrants, not batsmen. The 100-kilometre alternate-day commute from Samastipur to Patna echoes the journeys thousands of Indian families make to give their children a shot at something extraordinary.

Rajasthan Royals paid ₹1.1 crore for him at auction. Analysts now estimate his brand value alone exceeds ₹50 crore. Delhi Capitals, who dropped out of the bidding, will not make that mistake again.

## What Comes Next

Sooryavanshi has been named in India’s squad for the 2026 Asian Games, replacing the dropped Suryakumar Yadav. He turns sixteen in March 2027. The conversation is no longer about whether he will play international cricket — it is about when he will bat at number three for India in a World Cup.

His IPL season is over — Rajasthan Royals were eliminated in Qualifier 2 by Gujarat Titans. But the awards swept on Sunday night in Ahmedabad belong to a teenager from a small town in Bihar who made ninety thousand people at the Narendra Modi Stadium watch someone else’s trophy ceremony and think only about him.

“This season, I learnt how to play in pressure games,” Sooryavanshi said after collecting his final award. “You cannot play every game in one mode. You will have to read the situation of the game and play according to the requirements of the team.”

He is fifteen. He sounds like he has been doing this for a decade. Given his trajectory, he might be.
